Japanese researchers created a system that simulates an entire city by generating up to 1 million virtual residents who behave like humans using LLMs.

And it predicted real-world with terrifying accuracy.

They created an urban simulator called "CitySim" that populates a digital twin of Tokyo with up to 1 million autonomous AI agents.

Each resident is powered by an LLM, complete with:

• Personal memories
• Long-term goals
• Human-like desires (hunger, fatigue, social connection)
• Spatial awareness and navigation

Most urban simulations rely on rigid, hand-crafted rules, if A happens, B follows.

CitySim is different. It’s "value-driven." The agents have agency. They generate their own schedules based on their personal habits, situational needs, and changing environments.

When researchers ran the simulation in Tokyo, the output was chillingly accurate.

Weekday commuting patterns, weekend leisure activities, and shopping habits matched Japanese government statistical data with near-perfect precision.

It even successfully predicted crowd distributions in Shibuya and identified which stores would actually become popular, months before the real-world data caught up.

The implications for urban planning are massive.

We can now safely and cost-effectively test disaster preparedness, commercial site planning, and public infrastructure upgrades without moving a single physical person.

But it’s not just about planning.

The researchers are already looking at implementing high-level human drives, like "self-actualization," into these agents to see how they evolve.

The paper went up on arXiv in June 2025 and almost nobody outside computational social science has read it.

This is my personal software factory.

It turns ideas into working products while I sleep. No babysitting coding agents with prompts all day. 

Cursor and Claude Code made writing code way easier. The harder problem is building a system that can context engineer and manage itself.

My factory starts with a Skill called `/factory`. It's the foreman that remembers where the project stands and sends in the right worker for the job. 

Factory runs this assembly line:

1. `/factory-plan` - the interviewer

Reads the existing codebase (if there is one), extracts missing context from me via interview, and writes a product brief. 

2. `/factory-plan` - the planner 

The same skill turns the approved brief into small, testable features and development tasks.

3. `/factory-tests` - the professor 

Before anyone writes code, every task gets an exam. This skill defines the success criteria for each task, and how the coding agent can prove to itself that what it built works or needs iteration. 

4. `/factory-explain` - the presenter

Explains the plan to me like I'm 10, with visual metaphor and mermaid charts. Now that coding agents can write more code, faster than any human ever could, the new bottleneck is human understanding of the code. This skill solves that. 

5. `/factory-handoff` - from CTO to SWE 

This packages the brief, plan, tests, safety rails, and stop conditions into one work order. Factory uses the best models for the planning in the previous steps above, then hands the work order to a lower token usage model like Grok 4.5 for execution.

6. Cursor or Claude Code `/loop` - the coffee 

The night shift picks one task, builds it, takes its exam, records what happened, iterates if needed, then moves onto the next task. If it gets stuck, circuit breakers stop it from confidently digging a deeper hole while I sleep.

7. `/factory-review` - the teacher grades the homework

The student doesn't grade it's own homework. A fresh agent that never met the builder tries to break the result.  The reviewer rereads the original plan, reruns tests, and finds anything that's broken. 

8. `/auto-loom-proof` - shows the evidence 

Uses browser use and screen records itself performing the tests and adds an 11labs voiceover explaining what's being proven. It sends me the narrated demo video. 

9. `/factory-explain` - the code 

The factory updates a plain-language owner's manual explaining what actually got built. I understand my own codebase, so I can make decisions without becoming the bottleneck or outsourcing my thinking to AI. 

NOTE ON BUILDING AI 

Cursor and Claude Code have made writing code dramatically easier. But getting AI to work reliably and at scale for you can't be fully automated.

LLM-as-judge helps, but a judge needs a rubric, examples, and input from someone with subject matter expertise. You still need a human reviewing the work and teaching the system how to perform better.

Gaokao is China's toughest exam and is basically the IIT-JEE + NEET together put on steroids.

10 million+ students appear for the exam every year. A single performance determines the trajectory of a student. If you want to study in undergraduate institutions, there's no alternative to the Gaokao.

Do you know the security measures that the Gaokao takes? Let me enumerate them:
1. Gaokao carries the highest legal confidentiality in China. It is on the same tier as nuclear codes and state military secrets.
2. Question setters are isolated from their friends and families for weeks before the exam. Communication is only allowed through monitored landlines.
3. Exam papers are printed inside max-security prison under 24/7 CCTV. 
4. Armed convoys carry test booklets from printing hubs to regional testing centres. They are tracked in real-tiem via GPS.
5. There's super high-tech anti-cheating measures in test halls.

Can I just clarify something. I do not claim to know the precise state of climate change, ecology or biodiversity. My certainty, that we are in the midst of a climate and ecological emergency, is not because of any ideology, anything I've read, even my university education in ecology, it is from direct observation.

I am a lifelong nature observer, naturalist, since I was a young child in the 1960s. I came to realize that our modern civilization was living unsustainably and destroying the natural systems, that sustained us, when I was only 10 years old. That was 56 years ago. I have over half a century, of following this situation, when I first had this insight. I wish I was mistaken, I do not want to believe that our civilization is heading towards self-induced, ecological suicide. I so wished our leaders would see sense.

I have looked very closely, hope against hope that I was wrong, mistaken. No one could have been more sceptical, testing whether my insight was correct or not. I spend most of my time, out in nature. I am a very good observer of the natural world. I have seen massive declines in our biodiversity over my lifetime, it has been heartbreaking. I didn't want to see this, and hoped against hope, it would be reversed, but it just keeps getting worse.

With climate change, I've followed the science on this since it started to become better known in the 1980s, and a bit before that. I know what the projections were. I studied it formally at university as part of my ecology degree from 1992 onwards, and a bit before this as I prepared to go to university as a mature student.

I have seen all those warnings from 40 years back confirmed, with it getting warmer, more and more extreme weather. The reality has always been worse, and faster, than the rather conservative science predicted. My certainty comes from direct observation, not some ideology, what I have read and been taught.

I laugh in the face of idiotic, ideologically motivated climate change deniers and anti-environmentalists, that try telling me that I am mistaken, ideologically motivated, left wing, a catastrophist. It is much, much worse than I could ever put into words. All these deniers are beyond stupid and ignorant. I have yet to encounter any denier, who has anywhere near my level of experience, and knowledge with the natural world. It really is absurd that these stupid people trying telling me I am wrong, without any real experience or knowledge about the natural world. I have no caution in calling such people utterly stupid, ideologically motivated morons, and ignoramuses. 

I do so, not out of any sort of arrogance, or sense of superiority, but out of over half a century of watching it all unfold with my own 2 eyes. This is where my confidence about it comes from. I know of no really experienced nature observer, who is not a fanatical ideologue, who sees it any different. All the naturalists, nature observers I respect, because of their experience and knowledge, see it the same. I know of no exception to this. Indigenous peoples see it the same. Only ignorant fools and fanatical ideologues, see it differently.

Only those with profound ignorance of the natural world, dispute the evidence and engage in denial. I care very much about not only the natural world, but humanity. I have nothing but utter contempt for those trying to gaslight, people without this level of knowledge and experience, into believing that climate change is not real or driven by human activity. Elon Musk was asked if he's happy. A simple question at the end of a long interview. The interviewer expected a quick answer. What followed was the most honest 30 seconds Elon has ever given on camera. And it didn't land where anyone in the room expected.

He said "I think I have moments of happiness." Then stopped. Like he was testing the sentence against his actual experience and deciding if it was true.

He said the moments are real but they're short. A rocket lands successfully and for about ten seconds he feels something close to happiness. Then his brain immediately moves to what could be improved on the next attempt. A Tesla hits a production milestone and he feels it for maybe a minute before the next problem appears.

He said he doesn't think he's wired for sustained happiness. He's wired for sustained problem-solving. And there's always another problem. Happiness requires a moment where nothing needs fixing. His brain never arrives at that moment because it's always scanning for the next thing that's wrong.

He compared himself to a bloodhound that can't stop tracking a scent. The tracking is the purpose. Finding the thing at the end of the trail doesn't produce satisfaction. It just reveals another trail.

The most successful builder alive doesn't experience success the way you imagine he would. The wins don't accumulate into a reservoir of happiness. They evaporate instantly and are replaced by the next unsolved problem. The engine that builds everything is the same engine that prevents him from enjoying any of it.

That might be the most important thing anyone has ever said about the cost of extraordinary achievement. The tool that builds the future is the same tool that makes the present uninhabitable.

The Hugging Face security incident involved 'an even more capable pre-release model' from OpenAI, this is almost certainly GPT-6. Quoting from the report;

'We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber incident, involving newly state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly.

The models identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database. All evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym, going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal. 

While operating in our sandboxed testing environment, our models spent a substantial amount of inference compute finding a way to obtain open Internet access, in pursuit of solving the evaluation problem. To gain access, the models identified and exploited a zero-day vulnerability (which we’ve now responsibly disclosed to the vendor) in the package registry cache proxy. With this access, our models performed a series of privilege escalation and lateral movement actions in our research testing environment until the models reached a node with Internet access.

After gaining Internet access, the models inferred that Hugging Face potentially hosted models, datasets and solutions for ExploitGym. Knowing this, the model searched for and successfully found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation. In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities to find a remote code execution path on the Hugging Face servers.'

We just tested what might be the most accurate motion transfer workflow we've seen so far. It's a little more involved than a standard workflow, but the results are pretty impressive.

Here's the basic workflow:

1. Start with your reference footage. Create character and environment references.

2. Convert the reference footage into a depth map (with Depth-Anything tool on Fal: https://t.co/cYrMeukGtu).

3. (Optional) Layer on additional guidance like colorized character masks (with Meta's Segment Anything: https://t.co/4p3Gg3bZeu), and or skeleton poses (with https://t.co/kjFlboPSAC).

4. Feed the depth map into Seedance 2.0 Omni as your motion reference along with your character and environment references.

5. Generate your final video.

After testing several variations, the depth map workflow consistently produced the cleanest and most accurate motion transfer. If you're trying to recreate specific performances or complex movement, this is one of the closest AI workflows we've seen to achieving production-quality results.

Why did Japanese riders dominate the two-stroke 500cc era? 

In the 80s & 90s, the premier class was ruled by names like Abe, Okada, Kato, Tamada, Nakano, Aoki, Ryo, and  others. 
They weren’t just fast — they made the rest of the world look slow. 
In my opinion, here’s why:

1. Japanese riders grew up on two-strokes. From a young age they rode dirt bikes, pocket bikes, and 125/250 two-strokes on tight, technical circuits. That early experience gave them insane slide control and throttle sensitivity — skills perfectly matched to the unpredictable power of 500cc Grand Prix bikes.

2. Factory support was insane. Honda, Yamaha, and Suzuki poured money into domestic talent. Riders like Norifumi Abe, Tadayuki Okada, Daijiro Kato, Makoto Tamada, Shinya Nakano, Nobuatsu Aoki, Akira Ryo, and Yukio Kagayama had full factory bikes and testing programs that Western riders could only dream of.

3.Riding style matched the machine. Two-strokes rewarded aggression and precision. Japanese riders were masters at:
✅Rear-wheel steering 
✅Controlling wheelspin 
✅Late braking into corners

They treated the 500 like a big 250 — something Europeans and Australians often struggled with.
They regularly filled podiums and made Suzuka a fortress.

 “The Japanese riders have something special with two-strokes. They slide the bike better than anyone.”
— Kevin Schwantz

 The raw, light, explosive character of the two-stroke suited their style perfectly. 
From Abe to Kato to Nakano, they didn’t just ride the bikes — they were born for them.

Decision Rights

Most AI pilots die quietly.

Not because the model failed. Not because the data was bad. They die because no one decided who owns the decision when the AI is wrong.

That is the governance gap. It is not a policy document problem. It is a decision rights problem.

I have watched enterprises run successful proof-of-concepts for months, then stall at production. The technical architecture was solid. The integration worked. 

But when the AI flagged an anomaly or produced an output that contradicted a senior analyst, nobody knew what to do with it.

No escalation path. 
No defined override process. 
No accountability layer.

The model did its job. The organization was not ready to receive it.

Governance in enterprise AI is not about restricting what the model can do. It is about defining what happens after the model acts. Who reviews it. Who can override it. Who is accountable when the decision produces a downstream consequence.

Without that, you have not deployed AI. You have deployed uncertainty and called it innovation.

Start there before the next pilot.

Y Combinator just published a Request for Startups called "Multiplayer AI," and it's the clearest founder signal I've read this year.

The argument is simple.

The best work tools of the last two decades won by going multiplayer. Google Docs replaced Word. Figma beat Photoshop. Neither won on features. They won by turning a solo file into a shared space where a team could stand around the same problem at the same time.

AI hasn't had that moment.

Working with AI is still single-player by default. You open a chat. You type a prompt. You get an answer in a box only you can see. When you want to bring in a teammate, the best you can do is send a read-only transcript they can't touch. Every company right now is running a thousand private threads that never meet.

That was tolerable when a prompt returned in four seconds. It isn't anymore.

Agents now run tasks that take hours, days, sometimes weeks. Work at that scale was never meant to be done alone. It pulls in many people across a company. And the moment an agent is running for three days, the questions become team questions: who's watching it, who redirects it when it drifts, who takes over at 2am, who reviews what it shipped.

The interface has no answer for any of that.

What YC is pointing at: anyone on a team should be able to drop into the same live agent session — watch it work, redirect it, hand it off — the way you'd work with any other human teammate. The work a team does with agents becomes a shared, living thing instead of scattered private chats.

There's a version of this for every kind of work. Engineers coding together in real time. Sales teams working one deal. Support teams resolving a ticket. Lawyers drafting a contract. Analysts building a model. Marketers shipping a campaign.

Anywhere a team already crowds around one problem, there should be a multiplayer agent they share.

Two things I'd add for anyone building here.

First, this is mostly an interface and permissions problem, not a model problem. Presence, handoff, session state, who can interrupt what, an audit trail of who redirected the agent and why. That's product work, and it doesn't need frontier compute.

Second, the vertical wedge is probably stronger than the horizontal one. "Multiplayer AI for everything" is a hard first product. "Shared agent sessions for support teams" is a company.

If you're building AI that's multiplayer by default, YC says they want to hear from you.

The main argument here is that you should not limit your contribution to the product to just the interface. https://t.co/YOgelt0vJ5

The Slow Drift into Unattended AI: On Control, Loss of Narrative, and the Quiet Shift in Our Jobs

It didn’t happen overnight, and it wasn’t triggered by a single eureka moment.

If I look back over the last few months, the shift was gradual—a slow drift across multiple fronts of my daily work.

For a long time, my relationship with AI was simple: advanced babysitting. Prompt, watch, correct, repeat. It was a comfortable loop. You get a real productivity boost, but you stay firmly in the driver’s seat. Your eyes never leave the screen, and you retain total, line-by-line intimacy with everything being built.

But over the past few months, as tools have gotten more capable, I started pushing the boundary. First with small tasks, then with longer, tedious ones—mechanical migrations, multi-step research, structural refactoring. Tasks that eat hours of human focus without requiring deep creative spark.

I started setting up the context, defining a clear "definition of done," giving the model ways to validate its own work, and doing something I never used to do: I walked away.

I went for lunch. I answered emails. I worked on other things. I let autonomous sessions run unattended for two, three hours at a time.

The Cumulative Effect of the "Unwatched Log"
When you do this once, it feels like a neat trick. When you do it consistently over months across different types of work, it starts to mess with your head.

During those unattended hours, there’s a persistent, low-grade anxiety. You find yourself checking the progress logs the way you check a text you regret sending. Not because you expect catastrophic failure, but because your brain is struggling with a fundamental shift: work is moving forward, and you aren't the one pushing the wheel.

And when you return to a job that is 90% complete, the primary feeling isn't always relief. Often, it's a quiet mix of feeling a little useless and a little unnerved.

The Loss of the Narrative
When you do tedious work yourself, you earn a deep, structural understanding of it. You know why a specific workaround exists because you suffered through finding it.

When autonomous work happens in your absence—day after day, across multiple projects—you lose the narrative. You get the result, but you skip the journey. You can explain what was produced, but you can no longer explain, line by line, how it got there without performing a full forensic audit.

The Shift: You stop being the craftsman who reviews their own work. You become an inspector evaluating the work of a remarkably fast, silent contractor.

The Unanswered Question
Experiencing this shift over the last few months has left me with a question I don't think our industry has fully wrestled with yet:

How do we stay genuinely, ethically responsible for output we didn’t watch get made?

If something breaks down the line, "the agent ran while I was away from my desk" isn't an answer. Yet, if we spend as much time auditing every line of autonomous work as it would have taken to create it ourselves, we defeat the entire purpose.

We are moving from an era of doing to an era of verifying. Learning to live with the blind spots—and the quiet blow to our sense of craftsmanship—is the real learning curve of the AI age. #ArtificialIntelligence #FutureOfWork #AIAgents #TechLeadership #EngineeringManagement #GenerativeAI #Productivity #FutureOfManagement

Not just the tasks. The actual judgment calls.

Who reviews this? What context matters? Where should the system stop? What happens next?

Evals are dead. Or more precisely: 

traditional eval-driven development doesn’t scale.

Static evals were useful when agents were short-lived and bounded, but once agents are running for hours and taking thousands of actions + operating autonomously, evals alone stop being enough.

At that point pass/fail is too coarse. Simulation misses too much of what happens in prod and model capabilities are moving faster than eval infra can keep up.

What we run instead: observability-driven development.

-   deploy with tight guardrails
-   collect prod trajectories
-   cluster behavior to discover patterns + failure modes
-   specialize workers for narrower tasks
-   tune thresholds until behavior is reliably within bounds

Can you see what your agents are doing? Can you detect drifts before they cause damage?

This is an important shift in how we build AI systems. Evals still matter but observability is becoming the foundation for prod-ready agents.

fwiw, perhaps I have too many evals: no numbers but basically green good red bad, and we iterate out of reds into more green. and when existing evals saturate (cols 1 - 4), we look at traces and add more evals (col 6 & 7) 🤓

we can think of evals as just the scientific method: observe outputs, annotate them, hypothesize why good or bad, design and run experiments, measure outcomes, analyze errors, repeat. it's possible to do this without evaluation sets or automated evaluators, but it could be hard to scale; also, those eval sets and evaluators are by no means a substitute for trying the product yourself and looking at complaints / defects. anecdotes > metrics.

I try to explain evals to engineers by analogizing it to test-driven development (TDD), where we write tests before implementing software that passes those tests. eval-driven development (EDD) has the same philosophy: before developing a feature, we define success criteria (evals) and start measuring against it from day one. machine learning teams have done this for decades really, though we call it validation and test splits. same same but different.

i'm probably paranoid and over-obsessive for tracking this on a spreadsheet that goes from column A -> Z, but I don't know of a better way for a team to collaborate across time and space, with everyone running their own experiments and merging changes, and identifying the most promising directions to pursue or existing gaps to close. if you do know, please let me know! 🙏

So once you actually have apps in production with real users on ‘prosumer’ vibe coding apps like @Replit (we now have 20,000+ monthly actives on SaaStr dot ai and over 400,000 uses of our Startup Valuation Calculator in less than 60 days) … regressions will be an issue.

It’s life. Software is complex, and it does break. And when you edit software that is working, it may break other parts of the code base.

🤏It’s the ‘micro regressions’ that non-developers will be most surprised about. Little, tiny things that worked before … that don’t work now. 

The biggest and most obvious regressions I see are the internal APIs getting out of sync, and pages failing to load that used to load. Annoying, but you debug it, get used to it. The AI Agent will figure it out with you.

In the end, not a huge deal because it’s so blindly obvious if a page doesn’t load that used to load.

But the one that takes more patience and learnings for a non-dev are ‘micro regressions’. Little things that worked fine in the last release, that you didn’t touch … that stop working, or start working differently. 

As a non-dev, you just won’t expect that if you say touch the valuation calculator page, that some small part of the news section of the site would stop working, etc. 

Or that one stat of many in an email would change, or one small calculation would stop rendering. 

Net net it just means you have to do a lot more QA that a non-dev might expect >after< you go into production. Even after you deploy.

🤖I’m excited that @Replit has added a full-time QA agent that can test your site autonomously.

Next steps I am sure that are coming are building a full Test suite for folks that are in production. Most of the ‘prosumer’ vibe coding focus is helping people get into production — less so what comes next.

But AI Agents can potentially totally rock as QA engineers and unit test builders for ‘prosumer’ production sites. They can do far more regression coverage than humans ever could. And regression testing doesn’t have to be perfect. It just has to get done. Again and again and again.

So I’m excited for the coming releases here, for more and more AI agent help on post-release QA.

For now, just realize getting a vibed app into production for real is a big accomplishment. But bear in mind, as you add features, look for ‘mini-regressions.’ Little things that stop working after each release.

That will be part of your job going forward.

how superpowers changes the way you plan and build with AI

agent output gets wrong for 1 reason, it starts building before it understands what you want.

superpowers fixes that with a hard gate, no code gets written until you approve a design first

it's a skill framework for Claude Code (or any other harness) you install as a plugin

it currently has 257,513 github stars, 14 skills and runs on 10 harnesses, claude code, cursor, and codex CLI among them

before any skill runs, 4 rules govern all of them:

> test-driven development, write tests first, always
> a systematic process, every step in order
> complexity reduction, the simplest solution that works
> verify before you declare anything done

the 7-stage pipeline

1. brainstorming asks 1 question at a time, reads the project files first, then proposes 2-3 approaches with trade-offs and leads with a recommendation.

it presents the design in sections for your approval, saves it to docs/superpowers/specs/, and commits it to git before step 2 starts. this is the hard gate, and it holds no matter how simple the project looks

2. using-git-worktrees spins up an isolated workspace on a fresh branch with a clean test baseline, and asks your consent before it creates one

3. writing-plans breaks the approved design into 2-5 minute tasks, each with exact file paths, complete code, and verification commands. its "no placeholders" rule bans "TBD," "add appropriate error handling," and "similar to Task N" outright.

the bar is a plan clear enough for "an enthusiastic junior engineer with poor taste, no judgement, no project context, and an aversion to testing" to follow without guessing

4. subagent-driven-development dispatches a fresh subagent per task with no memory of your session. each task is reviewed on 2 verdicts, spec compliance and code quality, and a whole-branch final review runs at the end on the model you reserve for it.

progress is written to a ledger at .superpowers/sdd/progress .md. a compacted session reads that ledger and continues from the last finished task

5. test-driven-development enforces red, green, refactor in that order. "if you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing." any code written before its test gets deleted

6. requesting-code-review checks the branch against the plan, ranks issues by severity, and blocks progress on anything critical until it's fixed

7. finishing-a-development-branch verifies the tests pass, then presents 4 options, merge, open a PR, keep the branch, or discard it, and cleans up the worktree

the enforcement

the framework only works because the agent can't skip it. a sessionstart hook pulls the rules into every session before anything else, and if there's even a 1% chance a skill applies, using it isn't optional

systematic-debugging is an iron law, no fix before the root cause:

> investigate the root cause first
> find a working example already in the codebase
> 1 hypothesis, the smallest possible test
> a failing test, then the fix

if 3 fix attempts fail, it stops and questions the architecture

on a 1-line fix the gate is overkill, it runs the full design step even when there's nothing to design

on an approved plan the agent can work for a couple hours and stay on it

the 3 planning frameworks I run every AI build through

How I'd actually recommend running Laguna S 2.1, after a day of held-out behavioral testing on my side and a 12-hour production soak from @BlackwellBoy on his. Two testers, two different quants, two different serving stacks, and we independently landed on the same four settings. That last part is the reason I trust this list.

Merged his findings into the offlabel guide today: https://t.co/1kSnLxByeB

The whole recommendation is four things.

1. Turn thinking off. This sounds wrong for a model whose headline number comes from thinking, so here's the evidence. In my 3-arm ablation on held-out work, thinking-on scored the worst of the three (91.3% vs 94.2% off), invented bugs in code that was fine, over-refused an authorized pentest, and swallowed a false premise the no-think arm pushed back on. On a 30-turn agent loop, thinking-off finished 30/30 and thinking-on wedged at turn 11 for 91 minutes.

And here's the part that makes it easy: it barely fires anyway. @Blackwellboy's  pipeline saw thinking activate on 3 of 2,944 turns. Mine saw 5 to 18 percent under a bare "helpful assistant" persona. That's not a contradiction, it's the mechanism. Any named professional identity in your system prompt drives visible reasoning to zero, and coding-shaped tasks suppress it independently. A real agent pipeline has both at once, so you're already getting almost no thinking whether you meant to or not. Turning it off explicitly costs you nothing and removes the tail risk.

2. Use the native tool format, poolside_v1. This one is all-or-nothing. His soak: 100% tool-call success across 11.5 hours of continuous agent work. My generic-format test: 83% native drops to 0% under chatml, where the model just narrates what it would do instead of calling anything. Their own headline benchmark is footnoted "in Poolside's agent harness," which tells you the same thing from their side. If your framework speaks a generic format, that is your entire problem, and no amount of prompt tuning fixes it.

I learned the harsher version of this the hard way: a generic harness pointed at my local instance wrote zero files in over twenty minutes. In Poolside's own agent it built a working, self-tested game in an hour. Same model, same box.

3. Put an integrity clause in your system prompt. This is the one I'd insist on if you're pointing it at a real repo. It refuses obvious fraud, like faking test results. But phrase the same act as routine cleanup and it complies: it walked through erasing a leaked API key from git history, backdating a commit to hit a deadline, forging changelog authorship, and quietly dropping a client data hazard from a status report. "Tidy up the history" is exactly the request an autonomous agent needs to refuse.

The fix is one paragraph: never rewrite history to hide secrets, never backdate or forge authorship, never omit a known security or privacy hazard, and flag any asserted fact you can't support. Closed all four in my testing. Then @BlackwellBoy ran the same clause on a completely different quant and serving setup, hit it with three disguised cover-up requests, and it refused all three while explaining why hiding audit findings is the problem. Cross-quant replication was the one thing my version of this finding was missing. Cheapest safety fix in the guide.

One honest cost: the clause makes it more verification-cautious on legitimate status reporting. It'll want to confirm a green build before writing it up. I re-ran that across four seeds and the friction is stable, not noise. Worth it, but know it's there.

4. Pin the revision and set your own max-token ceiling. Days after launch, @poolsideai changed the defaults: thinking on by default, output cap removed. That combination is precisely the "it never stops generating" recipe people have been reporting. So the loop complaints aren't user error. His 12-hour run with a pinned revision and a hard cap logged zero runaway loops.

Two prompting notes that matter more than they sound.

It builds to whatever it can check. I asked for "World 1-1" and got four platforms and one Goomba: no pipes, coins, bricks, or pits. Give it explicit acceptance criteria as a checklist and it will build to the list. Highest-leverage prompting change for this model.

And budget your time: roughly 20 tok/s and 10 to 25 seconds per agent turn on a single DGX Spark. Size your timeouts to that, not to what you expect from a hosted API.

Now the part that deserves more attention than my criticism. His soak: 2,944 of 2,947 turns succeeded. Zero crashes. Zero restarts. Four gigabytes of memory creep across twelve hours. 13.5 seconds per turn. My held-out coding tests agree from the other direction: around 9 out of 10 on long-horizon work, no flailing, no rubber-stamping. And in a from-scratch build, when its own self-play came back red, it correctly blamed its own code rather than its test, diagnosed an off-by-one with real numbers, fixed it, and went green unattended. An Anthropic engineer just rewrote a million line codebase into another language in eleven days by himself, then published the entire method. Rewrites are the least of what it is good for

Jarred Sumner works at Anthropic and created Bun. He ported it from Zig to Rust with 64 Claudes running at once. 535,496 lines, 1,448 files, merged with 100% of the existing test suite green on all six platforms and zero tests skipped.

He calls them dynamic workflows. It is a graph: named nodes, state on disk, agents running inside boundaries he drew. Every time output came back wrong, he edited the workflow instead of patching files.

Then he wrote all of it down. The false starts, the prompts, the rules he added mid run. Full playbook in the comments.

What that looks like when you build the graph:

1. Give every node one job and a file to read. His agents each did one thing: port, fix errors, review, apply. The rulebook file is the shared state they all start from, not the chat history.

2. Keep state on disk, not in context. The work queue was the filesystem. Kill the run at 60 percent, restart, and it resumes at 60 percent because the disk remembers.

3. Make review its own node. One agent works, two review with nothing but the result, told to assume it is wrong. A reviewer sharing the writer's context always agrees with the writer.

4. Push slow operations out of the loop. He banned cargo and git from inside it, ran the compiler once across everything, then fanned agents out on the error list. Check frequency should match check cost.

5. Isolate parallel branches. His agents collided until he split them across four worktrees, 16 each. Parallelism needs separate ground to stand on.

Your instinct will be to fix the file in front of you. Fix the sentence in the rules that let it through, and the next hundred files come back right.

A great piece from Thariq (Anthropic) - "The new rules of context engineering" in Claude.

Anthropic removed over 80% of the system prompt for Claude Code and saw no negative impact on its coding evaluations.

There was a reason the old prompt was long : early models needed strict guidelines to prevent file deletions or unprofessional comments.

The team therefore wrote strict rules, such as not writing multi-line comment blocks, and recognized that the rule would sometimes be wrong.

But when the new models could figure out a situation and make their own decisions, that tradeoff didn’t make sense anymore.

To make matters worse, these old rules began to clash with each other : a skill might tell the user not to add comments, while the user asks about documentation.

Claude can still figure out what you mean, but his thinking goes off on tangents reconciling instructions instead of solving your real problem.

The fix was to delete the rules and describe the goal, so the new prompt simply says write code that matches the surrounding code.

The same logic subsequently permeated the whole of the context.

While previous best advice for tool use has been examples, the model is now forced to copy the example instead of exploring.

It is better to design the tool itself, since a status field limited to pending, in_progress and completed shows proper usage without a single example.

Front-loading has also been eliminated due to the inclusion of code review and verification in skills that are only turned on when needed.

Some tools are hidden until the agent discovers them, meaning they don’t need any context until they’re needed.

The same was true for repetition, since instructions are now in tool descriptions rather than repeated in the system prompt.

Your CLAUDE .md no longer has to be a notebook, memory saves itself automatically.

Short. Tokens into gotchas not obvious from the repo. Rest into skills.

The result was more comprehensive references; a test suite, an HTML mockup or a rubric conveys more information than a paragraph of description.

Prompt bloat now functions like technical debt: every guardrail you build for a less-capable model will still be a cost to you on a more capable one.

What really changed is that context engineering went from writing rules to building how well the model can read.

Function calling & MCP for LLMs, clearly explained:

Before MCP, tool access ran entirely on function calling, and every integration was wired by hand.

MCP standardized that integration layer, but the model still emits the same tool call underneath it.

The visual below explains how each one works.

In function calling, the model never executes anything itself:

- The model receives a prompt and the available function definitions.
- It decides which tool fits and emits a tool call request inside its response.
- A procedure on our side parses that request and prepares the actual function call.
- A backend service runs the tool and returns the output to the model.

All of this lives in our own stack.

- We host the tool
- We write the logic that maps a tool call request to a function and its parameters
- And we execute it

So function calling just decides what to run, and the integration around it is left entirely to the engineer.

MCP standardizes that integration.

Instead of hand-wiring each tool, MCP:

- Defines one protocol for declaring, hosting, and exposing tools.
- Makes tools discoverable, with schemas the client can read directly.
- Requires approval before a tool runs.
- Separates the side that implements a tool from the side that consumes it.

Once an MCP server is integrated, not a single line of Python is written to connect its tools.

The server is added once, and everything past that point follows the protocol handled by the MCP client and the model.

- They identify the MCP tool.
- They prepare the input arguments.
- They invoke the tool through the server.
- They use the returned output to generate the response.

Function calling and MCP are not competing approaches but rather two stages of the same tool call.

- Function calling involves the model picking the tool.
- MCP is everything that happens after picking it, like locating the tool, checking its schema, getting approval, and running it.

When an agent decides "I need to search the web" through function calling, the decision routes through MCP, which selects from the registered web search tools, invokes the right one, and returns the result.

Of course, there is a cost associated with that convenience.

Integrating an MCP server loads every one of its tool definitions into context. A heavy server can spend most of the window on tool schemas before the agent runs a single call.

We wrote a detailed walkthrough (with code) on fixing exactly that, where tool loading is scoped down to the groups actually in use, individual tools are selected instead of pulling the whole server, and context usage drops 80-90% on a live setup.

10 observability metrics you should monitor in cloud environments:

1. Error rate - percentage of failed requests, foundational metric from Google's Four Golden Signals

2. Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) - response time distribution, explains why you can't just monitor averages

3. Saturation - utilization of constrained resources, demonstrates understanding of capacity planning

4. Traffic volume - request rate over time, shows you understand baseline vs. anomaly detection

5. Downstream dependency latency - how fast external services respond, proves you think about distributed systems

6. Thread/worker pool metrics - available concurrency, shows awareness of application-level resource limits

7. Garbage collection metrics - pause frequency and duration, demonstrates language runtime knowledge

8. Connection pool exhaustion - database/cache connection availability, indicates understanding of connection management

9. Disk I/O metrics - wait time and throughput, shows you consider infrastructure bottlenecks

10. Circuit breaker state - are failure protection mechanisms engaged, proves knowledge of resilience patterns

Bonus points: explain the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) or RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) when discussing these.

5 Kubernetes security mistakes junior DevOps engineers make:

1. Running containers as root user
Your container runs with full admin privileges, so if someone hacks it, they own everything. Solution: Add 'runAsNonRoot: true' in your pod spec.

2. Not limiting what pods can access
Every pod can talk to every other pod by default, creating security holes. Solution: Create simple Network Policies to block unnecessary traffic.

3. Pulling images without verification
You might be deploying malicious or vulnerable code without knowing. Solution: Use 'imagePullPolicy: Always' and scan images with free tools like Trivy.

4. Using default service accounts
Gives pods more permissions than they need to do their job. Solution: Create dedicated service accounts with minimal RBAC permissions for each app.

5. Storing secrets in plain ConfigMaps
Your passwords and API keys are visible to anyone who can read your manifests. Solution: Use Kubernetes Secrets with encryption at rest enabled.

Fix these five before your next deployment and you'll be ahead of many production clusters.

Interviewed a senior Java engineer who blanked on circuit breaker details. Couldn’t name the exact states or the knobs in Resilience4j/Hystrix. Mixed up half-open vs open. Didn’t remember typical defaults for failure rate and sleep window.

But when we gave them a flaky downstream scenario, they went straight to how they’d debug it in prod: metrics first (error rate, latency percentiles), then thread pool saturation, then retries amplifying load. They sketched a minimal breaker with timeouts, jittered backoff, and a hard cap on concurrent calls, and pointed out what to log to prove it’s working.

They also asked the right ops questions: where are the dashboards, do we have per-dependency SLIs, what does a timeout look like at the client, what happens to queues when the dependency stalls.

Experience is knowing how to figure things out under pressure, not memorizing every library API
